newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CEOs welcome rise in yen as Rubin defends policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CEOs welcome rise in yen as Rubin defends policy.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin defended Washington's dollar policy Friday as business leaders, worried a strong dollar will hurt their ability to compete with Japanese firms, welcomed news the yen was rising.

Rubin spoke to the Business Council, a group of the nation's top corporate executives, about their currency concerns. He told them the U.S. policy was right and a strong dollar was good for the country.

"I think it has contributed to lower interest rates, I think that it has contributed to confidence in our markets and I think it has contributed to lower inflation," Rubin told reporters ahead of his closed-door talk to the chief executive officers.

The dollar has risen against major currencies the past two years but it has fallen against the yen in recent days. The decline accelerated Friday after comments in Tokyo on Thursday by a senior Japanese official that a stronger yen was possible given past foreign exchange fluctuations.

"Looking at currency fluctuations over the past 10 years, (the dollar-yen) moved at an annual average of 23 yen per dollar," senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara told a parliamentary panel on Thursday.
"This year, the yen weakened up to 127.50 yen to the dollar. If you subtract 23 yen, it is theoretically possible for the yen to strengthen to about 103 yen."
Rubin, who has said he shares Japanese government concerns about a weak yen, declined to say whether he shared Sakakibara's view.

"I wouldn't express a view of where it might go or what it might do," Rubin said. "I would just say we share their (Japanese) concerns about recent movements in the context of the G7 (group of seven industrial nations)."

Finance ministers and central bank governors of the seven leading industrial countries issued a statement in April after a meeting in Washington that said it was very important exchange rates not get out of sync with economic fundamentals.
The yen jumped to 120.20 yen to the dollar Friday from about 123.75 late on Thursday.

The change was good news for U.S. manufacturers, especially Detroit's big automakers, who have complained they were having a hard time competing in global markets against the Japanese because of the strong dollar.
A strong dollar makes U.S. goods more expensive around the world, as a weak yen makes Japanese goods cheaper.
Ford Motor Co. Chairman Alex Trotman, who attended the Business Council meeting, welcomed news that the yen had dipped Friday.

"From my point of view, as a very major manufacturer in dollars, I regard that as good news," Trotman told reporters after the closed-door session with Rubin. Each yen change has a "huge" impact on the bottom line of U.S. car manufacturers.

"I am feeling a little optimistic that with what we have been hearing ... that our voice is being heard," Trotman said. "I think that as a result of the things that have been said over the last few weeks, we are seeing some strengthening and I personally think that (the strengthening yen) is going to continue," he said.
AlliedSignal Inc. Chairman Lawrence Bossidy said as the meeting got underway on Thursday that he would welcome a level of 100 to 110 yen to the dollar.
"I think that makes competition more evenly balanced," he said in a television interview.
Yoshihiro Sakamoto, former vice minister of Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry, said Japanese companies could be competitive at 110 yen to the dollar.

But Trotman said that in the highly competitive automobile industry even that level would leave U.S. manufacturers at a disadvantage. "The best Japanese companies can be competitive at a lot stronger yen than 110," he said.
